transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-06-14
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Sana Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Li (Redwood SE), Markus Voss (Emberline VP Infra), Priya Rao (Lead Cloud), Liam O'Connor (Security), Ana Gomez (Platform)

Summary (auto):
Emberline is evaluating Redwood private onramp with strict egress controls and multi-region constraints. Main topics: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, transit gateway architecture, egress IPs, KMS/BYOK constraints, and timeline for pilot. Action items were identified and a lab test was proposed.

Topics: VPC topology, Private Endpoint handshake, Transit Gateway hub, Egress IP pinning, KMS integration, SOC2/ISO doc requests, Rollout timeline

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro from the Redwood side — I'm Alex, AE. Sana and Jordan are our SEs who will handle the hookup and tests.
[00:18] Markus Voss: Thanks Alex. I'm Markus, we run infra at Emberline. we have strong regs for patient PII so we need private-only traffic, no public egress for inference.
[00:30] Priya Rao: hi all, main ask is how Redwood's private offering will sit in our VPCs, what the network path looks like, and whether we can keep the control plane in a separate account.
[00:45] Sana Patel: totally, that's what we'll cover. quick question — are you leaning towards a transit gateway hub or direct VPC peering for connectivity?
[00:55] Priya Rao: we prefer hub-and-spoke with transit gateway for easier routing, but some teams want private endpoints (aws privatelink) to minimize route table changes.
[01:10] Jordan Li: okay, good. Redwood supports both patterns — we can do either transit gw attachment or PrivateLink endpoints. the tradeoffs are throughput and IP routing complexity.
[01:27] Liam O'Connor: interrupt, important compliance note — we require pinned egress IPs and a change window notice. can you provide stable NAT or egress IP ranges?
[01:40] Alex Chen: yes, we can provide a stable set of egress IPs for the private data plane. for Dedicated/Private deployments we typically support static egress blocks or a small set we publish and update during maintenance windows.
[01:55] Markus Voss: and BYOK? customer-managed keys? we cannot have provider-managed KMS keys for production PHI.
[02:05] Sana Patel: we do BYOK for Private. there's an HSM option for on-prem installs. we'll send the KMS integration doc but brief: control plane needs to be able to call key access for token exchange, but the data plane can be configured to decrypt locally if you run our private package.
[02:23] Priya Rao: sounds promising. can we get a diagram of the flow — which account holds the control plane and where the model runtime will live?
[02:33] Alex Chen: sure. for our hosted control plane model, control plane stays in Redwood's managed account, but for Private you can have a customer-managed control plane. we also support a split: customer-managed control plane with Redwood-managed runtime in your VPC.
[02:47] Jordan Li: to add, many customers go with customer control plane + private runtime inside their VPC for strict compliance — that keeps all egress internal.
[02:58] Markus Voss: ok that matches what we prefer. what about cross-region redundancy? we have users in EU and US, and data residency rules mandate EU inference for EU records.
[03:12] Sana Patel: we can pin workload routing by region. you can configure a policy that routes EU traffic to the EU-hosted runtime; the private endpoints must be in the EU region to satisfy residency.
[03:24] Priya Rao: is there any limitation on model sizes or throughput when running private in our VPC? we plan to run 16–32 sequence LLMs and need predictable latency.
[03:36] Jordan Li: mainly it's about the GPU allocation. Redwood Dedicated pools can be reserved; private runtime uses your infra so throughput scales with your instances. for predictable latency we suggest reserved Dedicated or fixed-size node groups.
[03:49] Liam O'Connor: network security specifics — we use strict egress rules with no direct internet outbound except via approved NATs. will Redwood agents require outbound to telemetry endpoints?
[04:02] Sana Patel: minimal telemetry is needed for health and metrics; however we can route telemetry over the private control channel or disable some telemetry in the initial pilot. we'll document the end points.
[04:15] Markus Voss: the devil's in the detail — we need an allowlist of IPs and FQDNs, list of ports, and an SLA for IP changes.
[04:27] Alex Chen: noted — we'll provide a network checklist with CIDRs, ports (443 primarily), and scheduled maintenance windows for changes.
[04:36] Priya Rao: when you say PrivateLink, is that inside our VPC or does Redwood provision the endpoint service on their side? how does the handshake work across accounts?
[04:49] Jordan Li: Redwood registers an endpoint service in our AWS account and you create an interface endpoint in your VPC and accept it. that keeps traffic on the AWS backbone and avoids route table peering.
[05:01] Priya Rao: do we need cross-account role trusts for mTLS? we prefer mTLS between services for extra security.
[05:11] Sana Patel: we can do mTLS for data plane connections; we also support mutual TLS using customer certs. for control plane auth we use OAuth2 tokens and can integrate with your IdP for the management console.
[05:23] Liam O'Connor: about audit logs — we need audit-level logging for each inference request (headers for who invoked). can Redwood provide request-level audit logs retained for 1 year?
[05:36] Alex Chen: we have configurable retention; for Private can push logs to your S3 or your logging endpoint, and retention is customer-managed. we'll include audit pipeline options in the doc.
[05:48] Markus Voss: great. can we talk about the initial pilot scope and what success looks like?
[05:55] Alex Chen: suggested pilot: 2-week lab in staging using replicable traffic, route traffic through your transit GW to a Redwood runtime in EU and US, validate latency SLOs, and validate egress pinning and KMS flows. success: <100ms P50 for short prompts and stable egress addresses, plus KMS BYOK working.
[06:12] Priya Rao: timeline-wise, we want pilot before end of Q3. headcount: our platform team will run the tests but security and infra need the docs and windows.
[06:23] Jordan Li: we'll need a bench account AWS creds for the test VPC, and a small node group we can use for runtime pods.
[06:31] Priya Rao: we can provision a staging VPC and give a cross-account role with limited perms for attachment.
[06:36] Alex Chen: perfect. okay, diving into specifics — CIDR planning: do you have existing CIDR blocks for the transit GW?
[06:44] Markus Voss: yes, we use 10.0.0.0/16 for the hub. spokes are 10.1.0.0/16 and upwards. we want Redwood to avoid overlapping ranges.
[06:55] Sana Patel: recommend that Redwood picks a /20 subset for our runtime to avoid collisions, and we can NAT outbound through your NAT gateway to pin egress.
[07:06] Liam O'Connor: question — if Redwood updates runtime nodes, could that change the egress IP within the pinned block? we need guarantees for short maintenance windows.
[07:19] Alex Chen: we typically keep egress within the published block; if a change is required we'll announce with at least 72 hours pre-notice for prod customers.
[07:30] Priya Rao: is there a way to host the runtime fully inside our account to eliminate dependency on Redwood-managed accounts?
[07:38] Jordan Li: yes, for Private deployments we offer a customer-owned runtime package that you deploy inside your account — it keeps everything inside your VPC and you control the nodes and the KMS keys. Redwood provides the operator manifests and support.
[07:52] Markus Voss: what about upgrades and patches? if it's customer-run, who triggers model upgrades?
[07:59] Sana Patel: typically the customer runs the runtime and decides when to roll model versions; Redwood can provide a managed upgrade path with a canary process if you want us to handle it.
[08:10] Ana Gomez: bandwidth/costs — inference traffic will incur cross-region egress charges. does Redwood provide tooling to estimate token count and egress bytes?
[08:23] Alex Chen: we have Redwood Optimize that estimates token usage and suggests batching and KV cache to reduce tokens. we'll share a small spreadsheet to model egress costs based on your expected traffic.
[08:34] Priya Rao: curious about network ACLs and interface endpoints — will the interface endpoint use private IPs from our ENIs?
[08:44] Jordan Li: yes, interface endpoints get ENI IPs in your subnets. you'll see connection attempts from those IPs; traffic doesn't traverse the internet.
[08:53] Liam O'Connor: for record — we require TLS 1.3 and mutual auth on data plane, and all EKS nodes must be in private subnets.
[09:03] Sana Patel: noted, we support TLS 1.3 and mTLS, and can provide Helm charts that assume private-only EKS nodes.
[09:12] Markus Voss: another operational ask — health checks and failover behavior. if a runtime in EU becomes unhealthy, will traffic fail to a US runtime? that's unacceptable for EU-residency data.
[09:25] Jordan Li: by default we can set a policy that prevents cross-region failover for EU-marked requests. you can also opt for multi-region deployment with regional routing rules.
[09:36] Priya Rao: okay good. also need to confirm DNS — internal FQDN patterns and if Redwood needs to manage a private hosted zone.
[09:45] Alex Chen: we can either publish internal SRV records for the endpoint or you can host private hosted zones and we provide the CNAMEs. we'll include both options in the diagram.
[09:55] Priya Rao: bandwidth shaping — some of our teams will want to limit QPS to protect underlying downstream services. can Redwood enforce per-route QPS and circuit break?
[10:06] Sana Patel: yes, per-route throttling and circuit breakers are supported at the gateway level. we'll show config examples.
[10:15] Markus Voss: on the legal side — we need a data processing addendum (DPA) plus SOC2 report and details about sub processors.
[10:24] Alex Chen: we'll send our DPA and the latest SOC2 Type II; for Private deployments subprocessor list is limited because you control the runtime.
[10:33] Priya Rao: small transcription aside — you mentioned HSM for on-prem. what does that look like? do you provide an HSM appliance or integrate with our HSM?
[10:44] Jordan Li: we integrate with customer HSMs and support common KMIP-compatible HSMs; if you need, Redwood can also provide a managed HSM gateway for the private control plane.
[10:55] Liam O'Connor: can we get more on key lifecycle: rotation, access logs, and separation of duties?
[11:03] Sana Patel: yes, docs will include rotation cadence, audit hooks, and RBAC mapping for key access.
[11:10] Alex Chen: quick note — we've got a short demo video of the PrivateLink handshake and a network checklist. I'll drop links after the call.
[11:17] Priya Rao: great. what's the typical time to stand up an initial private runtime in staging?
[11:24] Jordan Li: with infra ready and cross-account role in place, initial deploy can be done in 2–3 days; end-to-end pilot including validation and perf tests usually takes 2–3 weeks.
[11:33] Markus Voss: cost/back of envelope — we will estimate infra + Redwood license. do you offer pilot credits?
[11:40] Alex Chen: yes we often offer limited pilot credits for the platform fee; infra costs are separate. we'll include pilot pricing in the follow-up.
[11:49] Ana Gomez: question about logging — do logs cross account? we want logs to land in our S3 with server-side encryption using our KMS key.
[11:58] Sana Patel: absolutely; logs can be delivered to your S3 and encrypted with your keys. we'll include the handshake for the IAM role and S3 put policy.
[12:07] Priya Rao: one more on network: do you support AWS Private NATs or do you expect us to provision NAT gateways?
[12:16] Jordan Li: you provide the NAT gateway; Redwood routes through your NAT to pin egress. for some cloud providers we can offer managed NAT as an addon but typically customer-managed NAT is standard.
[12:28] Markus Voss: okay, think that's most of the network and security items. next steps?
[12:33] Alex Chen: we'll send the VPC design doc, the SOC2 and KMS integration guide, and the egress IP list. propose we schedule the lab handshake next Wednesday — does that work for the Emberline team?
[12:45] Priya Rao: yes next Wed works, we'll confirm exact time.
[12:50] Liam O'Connor: I'll collate the compliance Qs and share ahead of the lab.
[13:00] Alex Chen: awesome. wrapping up — recap: Redwood to share diagrams + docs; Emberline to provide staging VPC + egress IP constraints; schedule lab for next week; success criteria and pilot timeline agreed.
[13:14] Priya Rao: thanks everyone.
[13:16] Markus Voss: thanks.

Note: timestamps above mark the first ~13 minutes of discussion; the rest of the meeting covered deeper details and Q&A on the pilot checklist, a short walkthrough of the PrivateLink acceptance flow, and troubleshooting a simulated NAT failover scenario. There were occasional transcription inaccuracies (e.g., Redwood "Dedicated" heard as "Red wood dedicated") and a few speaker attribution swaps early on.

References shared in call:
- Network checklist (link): https://redwood.app/docs/network-checklist/emberline-stub

Action items (restated):
- Alex Chen: send VPC diagram + CIDR recommendations; include PrivateLink vs TGW pros/cons (due 2029-06-18)
- Priya Rao: provide staging VPC details, list of egress IPs, and access role for tests (due 2029-06-17)
- Sana Patel: prepare bench account and orchestration steps for runtime deployment (due 2029-06-20)

End of transcript.
